source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: Three field pretest-posttest studies at US transport agencies. Experts judged long-range (30 year) infrastructure investments before and after scenario work. No control group. Treatment: read a scenario, watch a video, discuss, vote on investments (100 points plus 1 to 3 vetoes), then see all scenarios and compare.
numbers: 3 or 4 scenarios per workshop; 10 to 15 experts per scenario; stratified random assignment to scenarios. Study I: 16 investments, state DOT. Study II: 15 investments, ocean port. Study III: 13 segment types, federal agency, 27 experts.
quote: management literature is devoid of rigorous studies that test the effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment
limits: No control group. Experts not accountable. One-time use, not the continual practice Shell uses.
agent_relevance: Best controlled-ish human evidence. A one-shot scenario pass changes judgments in a direction set by the scenario, but not confidence overall.

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: Study I: multiple-scenario use did not change aggregate confidence in investment calls, although more than half of judgments changed.
numbers: 343 pretest-posttest pairs; 189 (55.1%) judgments changed; confidence distribution pre vs post chi2=5.65, df=3, p=0.13. Highly certain 158 (46%) pre vs 157 (46%) post; somewhat certain 133 (39%) vs 120 (35%).
limits: Four-point confidence scale; no control for repeated testing.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a scenario step to lower the agent's confidence. Calibration needs its own check (G3).

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: Study II repeated the null on confidence with a finer 7-point probability scale. Judgments changed often but average confidence did not.
numbers: 285 pairs; 198 (69.5%) changed; mean confidence 0.811 pre vs 0.814 post, p=0.979 (paired t-test, two-tailed). Forced yes/no recommendation.
limits: Same design limits; no control group.
agent_relevance: Two instruments, same null: scenarios shift opinions, not certainty.

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: After one scenario, a changed judgment moved toward the scenario's verdict. Investments the scenario group voted useful became more favourable; wasteful ones less favourable. Neutral ones moved no more than chance.
numbers: Study II: 404 pairs, 288 (71.3%) changed. Useful: 62 judgments, 39 (62.9%) more favourable vs average 136/288 (47.2%), p<0.001. Wasteful: 70 judgments, 48 (68.6%) less favourable vs average 152/288 (52.8%), p<0.001. Neither: 75/156 (48.1%) more favourable, p=0.291. Useful rule: at least 1/n points and points >= 3x vetoes. Study I similar.
limits: Classification rule is arbitrary (authors ran sensitivity tests). Group vote in the same room may carry social influence.
agent_relevance: A scenario acts as a lens: the agent re-judges items to fit the lens it is given. Which scenario it gets matters more than how many.

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: High prior confidence resisted scenario-driven change. Experts who were highly certain before changed less often.
numbers: Study I: 419 pairs, 234 (55.8%) changed overall; highly certain 70/193 (36.3%) changed, p<0.001; about 7 in 10 changed at other confidence levels. Study II: 288/404 (71.3%) changed; certain experts 19/52 (36.5%), p<0.001.
limits: Authors say this may be a design artifact (a judgment at ceiling cannot become more favourable) or disconfirmation bias.
agent_relevance: A model already sure will not be moved by a scenario. Scenarios will not rescue overconfident answers; use a real check (G2, G3).

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: Study III: after multiple scenarios, experts shifted toward more flexible investment strategies, but most still picked the least flexible one.
limits: Authors offer urgency of the investment as a competing explanation, not tested. No control group.
agent_relevance: The one robust behavioural effect: scenarios push toward options that survive several futures. That is a rule code can check (robustness across scenarios).

source: Phadnis, Caplice, Sheffi, Singh (2015) Effect of scenario planning on field experts' judgment of long-range investment decisions, SMJ 36(9)
finding: The paper states the earlier experimental record: two studies, opposite results on confidence. The method is argued to cure overconfidence but this is not shown for experts.
numbers: Schoemaker (1993): MBA students widened confidence ranges after scenarios. Kuhn and Sniezek (1996): undergraduate psychology students were more confident after scenarios than controls.
limits: Phadnis blames design (control group or not) and task familiarity for the split. Both original studies are student samples.
agent_relevance: Effect on confidence is unstable across studies. Treat 'scenarios cure overconfidence' as unproven.

source: Kuhn and Sniezek (1996) Confidence and uncertainty in judgmental forecasting: differential effects of scenario presentation, J Behav Decis Making 9(4):231-247
finding: Lab experiment with a control group: scenario presentation raised confidence in five-decade forecasts of social issues (for example murder rate in Chicago, world population). Known only through Phadnis et al.; paper not read this session.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not read.
limits: Student sample, long-horizon almanac-style forecasts. Opposite direction from Schoemaker 1993.
agent_relevance: Warning: giving a model vivid scenarios can raise confidence, not lower it.

source: Schoemaker (1993) Multiple scenario development: its conceptual and behavioral foundation, SMJ 14(3):193-213
finding: Reported, via Phadnis, that MBA students broadened confidence ranges around point forecasts after scenario use. Schoemaker's 1995 article adds that asking for reasons for extreme outcomes may shrink ranges through incredulity. Original not read.
numbers: Not read. 932 citations (Semantic Scholar).
limits: No control group (per Phadnis). Student sample.
agent_relevance: Scenario plausibility matters: implausible extreme scenarios may be discounted.

source: Sheffi, Phadnis, Caplice (2016) How Scenario Planning Influences Strategic Decisions, MIT Sloan Management Review (summer)
finding: Practitioner summary of the field studies. Scenario users were almost equally likely to become more or less confident. Overconfident people are not necessarily humbled. Authors say results are for one-time use and the continual-practice effect is untested.
numbers: 158 confidence assessments before the workshop and 157 after (first study). Scenario build: 12 snapshot scenarios from a manager symposium plus survey.
quote: if you are overconfident about your own judgment, you won't necessarily become humbled
limits: Secondary report of Phadnis; one use only.
agent_relevance: Confirms the main caution: do not adopt a scenario operator expecting a calibration gain.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning
finding: Diffenbach (1983) found alternate scenarios were the third most popular long-range forecasting technique, used by 68% of the large organisations surveyed. This is an adoption figure, not an outcome figure.
numbers: 68% of large firms (as reported by Wikipedia; Diffenbach 1983 original not opened).
quote: there has only been anecdotal evidence offered in support of the value of scenarios
limits: Second-hand. Adoption is not effectiveness. 1983, US large firms only.
agent_relevance: Popularity is the only number; adoption is a weak reason to add the operator.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning
finding: De Geus's team audited scenario use at Shell in the early 1980s. The article says decision processes after the scenarios, not the scenarios, were the main cause of poor strategic implementation. Wikipedia tags this 'clarification needed' and gives no source.
numbers: No numbers. Shell analysts are said (citing Schwartz 1991) to credit scenarios for Shell becoming the largest in the world; Mercer (1995) reports the 1990s Shell CEO credited scenarios.
limits: Unsourced audit claim. Success claims are self-reports by Shell people. No counterfactual.
agent_relevance: The audit lesson fits our design: failure sits in follow-through, so code must carry the scenario result into action, not the model.

source: de Geus (1988) Planning as learning, Harvard Business Review
finding: Only the free opening was readable. De Geus says Shell planners surveyed 30 companies older than 75 years, and that Shell's own history shows swings between expansion and self-preservation. Scenarios and the audit are not in the excerpt.
numbers: 30 companies in business more than 75 years (survey; no method or results in excerpt).
limits: Paywall: the argument on scenarios was not read. The audit claim cannot be confirmed here.
agent_relevance: The primary source for 'planning is learning' is not open; do not quote beyond the opening.

source: Wack (1985) Scenarios: uncharted waters ahead, Harvard Business Review 63(5)
finding: Only the opening was readable. Wack says forecasting errors became more frequent and sometimes huge since the early 1970s, and that he developed the Shell scenario system. The oil-shock case is not in the readable part.
numbers: None.
quote: forecasting errors have become more frequent and occasionally of dramatic and unprecedented magnitude
limits: Paywall. Founding claims are narrative, not data.
agent_relevance: Founding claim is anecdotal case evidence; no effect size exists in it.

source: Schoemaker (1995) Scenario planning: a tool for strategic thinking, MIT Sloan Management Review
finding: Argues scenarios counter three biases: anchoring on the status quo, availability, and overconfidence in narrow ranges. Cites Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980): generating reasons can improve calibration. Notes reasons for extreme outcomes may shrink ranges through incredulity. Reports no experiment of its own.
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes in the text.
limits: Theory and cases (GM, IBM, DEC). Mechanism claims, not tests.
agent_relevance: The theory behind the operator: widen the range by forcing structured alternatives. Evidence in experts is mixed (Phadnis).

source: Glick, Chermack, Luckel, Gauck (2012) Effects of scenario planning on participant mental models, Eur J Training and Development 36(5):488-507
finding: Single-group pretest-posttest on a mental-model style survey. Scenario planning raised efficiency, social and systems styles with moderate effects. Full statistics not seen (paywall).
numbers: 129 participants from 10 organisations; paired t-tests on 5 factors; no control group; exact t and d not seen.
limits: No control group; self-report survey; demand effects likely. Authors call for control groups.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for 'changes mental models'. Self-report is not decision quality.

source: Meissner and Wulf (2013) Cognitive benefits of scenario planning: its impact on biases and decision quality, Technol Forecast Soc Change 80(4):801-814
finding: Experimental test of scenario planning on biases and decision quality. Only metadata and the 85-item reference list were read (Crossref), so results are unknown here. References show it builds on framing, counterfactual mind-sets, anchoring, illusion of control and overconfidence in interval estimates.
numbers: Not read. 142 citations (Semantic Scholar).
limits: Closed access.
agent_relevance: Needs a second pass: the main lab test of bias reduction. Do not cite results until read.

source: Phelps, Chan, Kapsalis (2001) Does scenario planning affect performance? Two exploratory studies, J Business Research
finding: Two exploratory studies of the link between scenario planning and firm performance. Not read; no result claimed here.
numbers: Not read. 111 citations (Crossref).
limits: Title says exploratory. Correlational firm data cannot show cause.
agent_relevance: Needs a second pass: the only firm-performance study on the list.

source: Futures and Foresight Science (2022) The value of experiments in futures and foresight science as illustrated by the case of scenario planning
finding: Abstract only (via Semantic Scholar). Argues experiments on foresight tools are valuable, that conceptual and direct replication should be told apart, and that the unit of analysis needs care. Scenario planning is the worked example. Signals few direct replications exist.
numbers: None in abstract. 13 citations.
limits: Abstract only; Wiley blocked full text.
agent_relevance: Supports our caution: the experimental base is thin and rarely replicated.

source: Rohrbeck and Kum (2018) Corporate foresight and its impact on firm performance: a longitudinal analysis, Technol Forecast Soc Change
finding: Longitudinal analysis linking corporate foresight maturity to firm performance. Not read; headline numbers not verified this session. Foresight is broader than scenarios.
numbers: Not verified. 290 citations (Crossref).
limits: Correlational; foresight includes many practices; reverse causation open.
agent_relevance: If read, the best firm-level association for 'foresight pays'; still not scenario-specific.

source: Csaszar, Peterson, Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a Fully Prospective Venture Tournament, arXiv:2602.01684
finding: Prospective forecasting test, not a scenario-planning test. LLMs and humans ranked 30 live Kickstarter tech projects by eventual fundraising success before outcomes were known.
numbers: 30 projects launched after all model cutoffs; 870 pairwise comparisons per LLM (double round robin); 346 managers from Prolific; 3 MBA-trained investors. Metrics: Spearman rank correlation, pairwise accuracy, value capture.
limits: Preprint draft marked do-not-cite. 30 items only. Narrow task. Wide confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: LLMs can rank uncertain ventures better than managers; this says nothing yet about the scenario method.

source: Csaszar, Peterson, Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a Fully Prospective Venture Tournament, arXiv:2602.01684
finding: Frontier LLMs beat humans on rank correlation. Best LLM Gemini 2.5 Pro; GPT-5 family 0.67 to 0.71. Best human 0.45. The Prolific crowd and one expert were indistinguishable from zero.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Pro rho=0.74; GPT-5 family 0.67 to 0.71; Expert 3 0.45; Prolific crowd 0.19; Expert 1 0.04. Gemini minus Expert 3 = 0.29, p=0.063. Pairwise accuracy: Expert 3 67%, Prolific 56%, Expert 1 about 52%.
limits: Gap to best human not significant at 0.05 (p=0.063). Three experts only.
agent_relevance: Base rate for our agent: a strong plain model already forecasts well; a scenario step must beat that.

source: Csaszar, Peterson, Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a Fully Prospective Venture Tournament, arXiv:2602.01684
finding: Value capture was bimodal. Crowd ensembles and human-AI hybrids did not beat the best single model.
numbers: Twelve evaluators (all LLM or Prolific) captured more than 83% of oracle value; random 18.9%; all others below 50%. Prolific 85%, the only human group significantly above chance.
limits: Top-K=5 selection rule; skewed outcomes (authors' footnote).
agent_relevance: Supports G4: extra voters or combinations do not beat the single best forecaster.

source: Csaszar, Peterson, Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a Fully Prospective Venture Tournament, arXiv:2602.01684
finding: Gap statement: this paper tests judgment of unknown outcomes with no scenario-planning arm. No LLM study found this session tests the scenario method against a no-scenario control on a measured outcome.
numbers: None.
limits: Search was limited: web search budget ran out after 2 calls; arXiv API returned empty; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Evidence for adding a scenario operator to an LLM agent is missing, not negative. Test it ourselves (A/B on a held-out set).

source: Jungwirth and Haluza (2023) AI-Based Scenario Generation for Future Planning: An Exploratory Study Using GPT-3, J Curr Trends Comp Sci Res 2(2):57-67
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003, data to June 2021) was asked for Ukraine scenarios with probabilities, without the war being named. It gave four scenarios, one describing open war. Authors judged its predictive power limited and its scenario consistency improvable.
numbers: Four scenarios; stated probabilities: 40% Russian forces stay in control, 20% full-scale war, 10% international intervention; first scenario appears to be 30%. Self-reported consistency: 100% for two scenarios, 66.67% for one. Temperature 0.7, 3,500 max tokens, penalties 0.5.
limits: One prompt, one topic, one model; no baseline or control; one hindsight check against UN pages; consistency scored by the same model.
agent_relevance: One case. The realised outcome got 20% and was listed, a modest hit.

source: Jungwirth and Haluza (2023) AI-Based Scenario Generation for Future Planning: An Exploratory Study Using GPT-3, J Curr Trends Comp Sci Res 2(2):57-67
finding: Method note: the same model generated the scenarios, scored their driver consistency and approved the manuscript. Authors asked GPT-3 to confirm co-authorship and it agreed.
numbers: Stage-gate with 4 gates; measurable outcomes rated no, yes or partly as of 21 Feb 2023.
limits: Model grading its own output; no independent check.
agent_relevance: Matches our rule that the model never grades its own answer without a check (schema section 1).

source: XFinBench: Benchmarking LLMs in Complex Financial Problem Solving and Reasoning, arXiv:2508.15861
finding: Search listing only: a 4,235-example finance benchmark where top models trail human experts, especially in temporal reasoning and scenario planning. 'Scenario planning' here is a finance question type, not Shell-style scenarios.
numbers: 4,235 examples (listing). Model scores not read.
limits: Not read; different meaning of scenario planning.
agent_relevance: Weak link only; do not count as evidence for the method.

source: Strategy Science (2026) experiment on AI-augmented strategic foresight under time constraints, doi 10.1287/stsc.2025.0442; Picavet et al. (2025) Public Administration Review scenario pilot
finding: Known only from a web-search summary (publisher pages blocked). Strategy Science: 348 participants; time limits and LLM use did not change foresight accuracy, but LLM use increased breadth, decreased depth and reduced consensus. Picavet pilot: said to cut staff hours 60 to 70% and give eight scenarios vs four, per a university summary, not the paper.
numbers: 348 participants (secondary). 60 to 70% staff hours; 8 vs 4 scenarios (secondary, unverified).
limits: Not opened. Secondary summary only; check before use.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, LLM scenario help saves effort and adds breadth but not accuracy, matching the Phadnis pattern.
